Lessons.Title: Writing Equations to Model Relationships (Part 2)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: infer relationships in tables of values, distinguish additive, multiplicative, constant-total and inverse-variation patterns, and write an equation with appropriate variable domains. First-party independent Edulytiks adaptation based on Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 2 Lesson 3, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/3/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Publisher roles: Addressing HSA-CED.A.2 and HSA-CED.A.3; Building Towards HSA-CED.A.2 and HSF-LE.A.2. The source requires persevering with novel patterns rather than memorizing one generic linear formula.

Original tables to classify: A has x=0,1,2,4 and y=3,8,13,23, following y=5x+3; B has x=0,25,100,175 and y=400,375,300,225, following x+y=400; C has positive x=1,2,3,6 and y=48,24,16,8, following xy=48. All relationships are real-number mathematical models under stated domains; table C cannot use x=0 because the inverse model is undefined there.

First decide what remains invariant in each row: for A, each +1 in x means +5 in y, with initial y=3; for B, the sum x+y remains 400; for C, the product xy remains 48 even when differences or ratios of corresponding terms change. Tables alone may fit many arbitrary rules, so model choice also depends on a meaningful context and assumptions.

Context tasks: a bike rental costs $3 start charge and $5 per hour, with x≥0 hours (A); two distances from opposite ends of a 400-metre straight trail add to 400, with 0≤x,y≤400 (B); a rectangle of area 48 square centimetres has width x>0 and height y=48/x>0 (C). For a model involving prizes split equally, the number of winners must additionally be a positive integer.

Student activity: work from an unknown table, propose and reject candidate equations, extend it to an unlisted input, construct a matching word problem, and critique a partner's table or graph for units and restrictions. Teacher-scored rubric 0–2 points each for table differences/products, correct equation and domain, checked predictions, and valid contextual explanation (maximum 8). Avoid auto-grading a unique formula as the only possible mathematical description of finitely many points.

V13 source reconciliation: source U2L3 asks students first to infer a novel table rule, then MATCH FOUR contextual tables to four distinct equations: multiplying by a fixed rate, adding an offset, subtracting an offset, and a fixed combined total. The original lesson described only three candidate patterns and did not give an explicit four-way equation-matching task.

V13 independent four-card sort (not publisher numbers): A (x,y)=(0,0),(1,300),(2,600) -> y=300x; B (0,300),(20,320),(40,340) -> y=x+300; C (300,0),(360,60),(420,120) -> y=x-300; D (0,300),(90,210),(275,25) -> x+y=300. Shuffle rules separately; students justify unit-consistent contexts, all sample rows, and a value not shown. Additionally retain the earlier constant-area rectangle xy=48 for positive dimensions and explain why it is an inverse rather than linear rule.

KeyConcepts.Title: Additive and multiplicative invariants
KeyConcepts.Definition: A constant difference, constant sum or constant product identifies a possible structural relationship.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check several rows before guessing the equation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Linear table pattern
KeyConcepts.Definition: For y=mx+b, equal increments in x lead to proportional changes in y, with y-intercept b.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check slope (Δy)/(Δx) on multiple intervals, including unequal step sizes.
KeyConcepts.Example: x=0,1,2,4 gives y=3,8,13,23: slope always 5, intercept 3.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inverse relationship and domain
KeyConcepts.Definition: For xy=k, positive k and x>0, y=k/x decreases as x increases.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The domain must exclude x=0 and use positive lengths for geometric context.
KeyConcepts.Example: x=3 yields y=16 cm for area 48 cm².

WorkedExamples.Title: Infer a linear rule with unequal steps
WorkedExamples.Question: Find a rule for (x,y)=(0,3),(1,8),(2,13),(4,23).
WorkedExamples.Method: Compute slopes for consecutive table intervals and use the row at x=0.
Steps: From x=0 to 1, Δy=5 and Δx=1, giving slope 5.
From x=1 to 2, slope is again 5.
From x=2 to 4, Δy=10 over Δx=2, giving slope 5.
Propose y=5x+3 and verify x=4 gives 5×4+3=23.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A natural linear rule is y=5x+3.
WorkedExamples.Check: All four pairs satisfy the rule; finite points alone cannot prove uniqueness among arbitrary functions.

WorkedExamples.Title: Model a constant total
WorkedExamples.Question: A straight path is 400 metres. Distance x from one end and y from the other sum to 400. Find y at x=175.
WorkedExamples.Method: Represent the conserved total and solve the equation.
Steps: State domain 0≤x≤400, 0≤y≤400 for points along the path.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both distances are nonnegative and total exactly 400 metres.

WorkedExamples.Title: Infer an inverse model
WorkedExamples.Question: A rectangle has area 48 cm². Width x is 6 cm. Find height y and explain why x cannot be zero.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use the invariant product of lengths.
Steps: For x=6 cm, solve 6y=48, so y=8 cm.
General rule y=48/x for positive width x.
At x=0 division is undefined and a zero-width rectangle cannot have positive area.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Height y=8 cm and model domain x>0.
WorkedExamples.Check: The units cm×cm = cm² and the positive-length domain is satisfied.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming equal changes in x always mean equal changes in y
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Inverse and other nonlinear relationships may have constant products rather than differences.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Test sums, differences, products and ratios against several rows.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Division by zero is undefined and violates the positive-area context.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Restrict x>0 for positive rectangle dimensions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating finitely many table values as proof of a unique function
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Different functions can agree on listed points but differ elsewhere.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State and justify the simplest source-relevant model and its real-world assumptions.

SummaryPoints: Look for constant slopes, constant sums or constant products, then verify against every row.
A: y=5x+3; B: x+y=400; C: xy=48 with x>0.
Context imposes restrictions on allowed inputs, outputs and units.
Different tables need different reasoning; model selection and partner explanations require teacher assessment.
